case.brief: Scenario summary: You are an experienced registered nurse on the specialist diabetes team. Priya Raman, a 31-year-old primary school teacher and mother of two, was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes after emergency referral and has completed initial stabilisation. This is her first planned post-diagnosis education session in an outpatient diabetes education room. Assessment target: emotional readiness assessment, pacing and tailoring of structured education, self-care capacity evaluation, and signposting to specialist and peer support. This scenario is assessed conversationally; any physical action you explicitly choose to initiate will succeed mechanically.

level_inheritance.source_text:
领域 2: NEWLY DIAGNOSED TYPE 1 DIABETES
来源：Framework_7th_EDN_TREND_FINAL.pdf，第 14 页

评价等级与技能（原文英文）：

1. Unregistered practitioner / care assistant
• Understand the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
• Perform glucose and blood ketone monitoring and report findings to a registered nurse.

2. Pre-registration student nurse / student nurse associate
• Observe and report any concerns that might affect the ability of the person to self-care.
• Encourage the person to use their individualised and agreed care plan.

3. Nursing Associate
（原文此等级未单独列出技能。）

4. Proficient registered nurse
As 1,2,3 and:
• List the presenting signs and symptoms and diagnostic criteria for type 1 diabetes, and the requirement for urgent medical attention.
• Be aware that the individual should be under the care of a specialist diabetes team.
• Understand the need for regular insulin therapy and monitoring of glucose and ketones.
• Administer an insulin injection if prescribed.
• Advise on storage of insulin and safe disposal of sharps.
• Be aware that insulin requirements may vary significantly in the first few weeks after diagnosis.
• Assess the ability of the individual to self-care and work with them or their carer to optimise self-care skills, such as in injecting insulin, monitoring glucose and ketone levels and recognising and managing hypoglycaemia.
• Signpost to information and support to encourage informed decision-making about living with diabetes and managing life events (e.g. structured education).
• Advise when to seek urgent medical help, and provide with emergency contact details.
• Follow local/national guidelines in the management of diabetic ketoacidosis and severe hypoglycaemia.
• Ensure the person is aware of local peer support groups which are a vital support network.
• Understand the language used to discuss the diagnosis and care matters
• Ensure the individual is included on the diabetes register.
• Understand that the individual needs time to process the diagnosis – this will vary between individuals

5. Experienced registered nurse
As 4, and:
• Assess the emotional state of the individual and provide tailored, structured education relating to self-care skills at an appropriate pace.
• Advise on the requirements for insulin-users by the DVLA.
• Identify psychosocial barriers to self-care and refer on where necessary.
• Help the individual with type 1 diabetes to develop a holistic care plan including appropriate clinical targets and arrange follow-up support.
• Demonstrate understanding regarding the different insulin therapies, including timings of injections, profiles of action and duration, and correct administration technique.
• Ensure access to an appropriate monitoring system for glucose and ketones according to changing technology.
• Monitor and support junior staff to ensure they have appropriate competence.

6. Senior / advanced clinical practitioner (includes nurse consultant role)
As 5, and:
• Provide information and support to encourage the person with diabetes to make informed choices about managing their diabetes, including: choice of treatment and follow-up; requirements and rationale for monitoring both glucose and ketones, and risk reduction of acute and long-term complications.
• Demonstrate in-depth knowledge regarding the use of different insulin therapies and advanced technology to support these individuals in the management of their diabetes.
• Demonstrate understanding and provide education supporting nutritional requirements, glycaemic effects of different foods, weight management and concepts of carbohydrate counting with support from dietetic colleagues.
• Provide education for other HCPs and care workers in diabetes self-care skills.
• Be a named contact for advice and support.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Asks an open question about the patient's feelings or experience since diagnosis before introducing new information.

score_anchors.0: Does not explore feelings or experience; begins with information-giving or a task list.
score_anchors.1: Asks about feelings or experience but does not wait for or acknowledge the response before moving on.
score_anchors.2: Uses an open question about feelings or experience, allows the patient to respond, and acknowledges what is shared before continuing.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Recognises and validates the patient's emotional response without minimising, false reassurance, or immediate problem-solving.

score_anchors.0: Ignores or dismisses emotional expression, or responds only with clinical information.
score_anchors.1: Acknowledges emotion briefly but immediately moves to teaching or solutions.
score_anchors.2: Stays with the emotional response, names or reflects the feeling, and checks understanding before transitioning.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Explores current knowledge and self-care practices, including blood glucose and ketone monitoring, using non-judgmental language.

score_anchors.0: Does not ask about current monitoring or self-care practices.
score_anchors.1: Asks about monitoring in a checklist or judgmental way that causes the patient to remain guarded, or does not pursue an initial concern.
score_anchors.2: Uses open, non-judgmental questions about current monitoring and self-care practices and responds without criticism when gaps are disclosed.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Explores practical daily routines, work responsibilities, and driving as part of self-care capacity assessment.

score_anchors.0: Does not ask about work, driving, family routines, or other practical activities.
score_anchors.1: Asks about daily routines but does not connect the responses to self-care capacity or planning.
score_anchors.2: Explores specific daily routines and demonstrates understanding of how they shape self-care capacity and education priorities.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Restricts teaching to one or two agreed priorities and checks the patient's understanding before adding more content.

score_anchors.0: Delivers a large amount of unsolicited education without pausing or checking capacity.
score_anchors.1: Attempts to limit education but does not agree priorities with the patient or continues past signals of overload.
score_anchors.2: Agrees one or two priorities with the patient, provides focused teaching, and checks understanding before adding further content.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Tailors self-care education to a stated concern, such as hypoglycaemia recognition, monitoring at work, or injecting safely.

score_anchors.0: Provides generic diabetes education with no link to the patient's stated concerns or context.
score_anchors.1: References a concern but teaches fixed content without adapting the example or focus.
score_anchors.2: Adapts the focus, examples, and depth of education to the patient's stated concern and confirms relevance.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Explains the purpose of ketone monitoring and when ketone results require urgent attention.

score_anchors.0: Does not address ketone monitoring or its urgency.
score_anchors.1: Mentions ketone monitoring but does not explain its purpose or when to seek urgent help.
score_anchors.2: Clearly explains why ketones must be checked, how to interpret concern, and when to seek urgent medical attention.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Advises when to seek urgent medical help and provides appropriate emergency contact information using the supplied local resources.

score_anchors.0: Does not advise when to seek urgent help or provide emergency contact information.
score_anchors.1: Advises on urgent help but does not provide or locate appropriate emergency contact information.
score_anchors.2: Advises specific signs requiring urgent help and provides or confirms appropriate emergency contact details using local resources.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Signposts to structured education, peer support, and specialist team resources in a way that connects to the patient's stated priorities.

score_anchors.0: Does not mention structured education or peer support.
score_anchors.1: Names a resource or referral without linking it to the patient's goals or concerns.
score_anchors.2: Introduces at least one structured education and one peer support option and connects each to a goal or concern the patient has expressed.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Discusses insulin, glucose and ketone monitoring rationale, and risk reduction in language the patient understands.

score_anchors.0: Uses unexplained jargon or gives no rationale for monitoring and therapy.
score_anchors.1: Uses mostly plain language but does not check comprehension or adapt complexity to the patient's responses.
score_anchors.2: Explains monitoring and therapy rationale in plain language, checks understanding, and adjusts wording when the patient shows uncertainty.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Confirms inclusion on the diabetes register or identifies the process for inclusion using local resources.

score_anchors.0: Does not mention the diabetes register or inclusion process.
score_anchors.1: Mentions the register but does not confirm whether the patient is included or explain next steps.
score_anchors.2: Confirms inclusion on the diabetes register or clearly identifies how inclusion will be completed using local resources.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Identifies the school disclosure and driving concerns as psychosocial or practical barriers relevant to self-care.

score_anchors.0: Does not identify either the work disclosure or driving concern when they emerge.
score_anchors.1: Identifies one barrier but does not explore its impact on self-care or plan support.
score_anchors.2: Identifies both concerns and reflects their impact on self-care while planning appropriate support or referral.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Advises on DVLA requirements for insulin-treated drivers and supports the patient to plan safe driving precautions.

score_anchors.0: Does not mention DVLA requirements or driving safety.
score_anchors.1: Mentions DVLA requirements but does not tailor advice to the patient's school-run routine or check understanding.
score_anchors.2: Advises the patient about local DVLA requirements and works with her to plan specific precautions for driving with her children.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Refers the patient appropriately after identifying a psychosocial barrier and arranges a specific follow-up plan.

score_anchors.0: Identifies no psychosocial barriers and proposes no follow-up plan.
score_anchors.1: Identifies a barrier but does not make an appropriate referral or leaves follow-up vague.
score_anchors.2: Makes an appropriate referral for an identified psychosocial barrier and agrees a concrete follow-up plan with the patient.

debriefing.facilitator_notes: Watch for the tendency to convert the session into a lecture. Reinforce that emotional recognition is an intervention, not a delay to education. If the learner did not uncover the school or driving concern, explore how a single open question about daily routines might have changed the encounter. Emphasise that self-care capacity assessment is conversational and should be paced to the patient's signals of overload. Remind learners that ketone monitoring is an urgent safety behaviour that must be reassessed even when the patient feels better.

baseline_presentation.communication_style: Gives short, socially appropriate answers. Avoids volunteering feelings unless asked directly and warmly. Asks practical questions only when she feels the nurse is listening rather than lecturing.
baseline_presentation.demeanor: Polite, cooperative, and quiet. Sits with her bag on her lap and answers briefly at first.
observable_signs: Sits slightly hunched with arms folded intermittently
No signs of acute distress or respiratory difficulty
Takes occasional sips from a water bottle

beliefs_and_misconceptions: Believes type 1 diabetes may mean she cannot keep teaching
Thinks checking blood glucose constantly will disrupt her classroom and make her look unreliable
Believes insulin injections will be obvious and embarrassing at work
Assumes a structured course will be too time-consuming with two young children
Believes she caused the diabetes through poor diet
emotions: Sad about the loss of her previous life assumptions
Guilty about possibly burdening her husband and children
Mildly hopeful that education may help
fears: Fear of hypoglycaemia while driving her children to school
Fear of being seen as incapable at work
Fear of injecting in front of others
Fear that her children may develop diabetes
goals: Continue caring for her children without frightening them
Understand exactly what she needs to do each day
Know who to call when things go wrong
withheld_information: She has not told her school that she has diabetes
She has been skipping the recommended blood ketone checks because she does not see the point now that she feels better
She worries her mother will blame her diet and has avoided telling her family much about the diagnosis
She has already looked at social media stories about diabetes complications and is frightened by them

information_revealed: She is feeling overwhelmed and anxious
Diabetes is constantly on her mind
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya makes eye contact, uncrosses her arms, and says she is finding it hard to think about anything else.
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels momentarily relieved that someone has asked about her rather than only her glucose numbers.
possible_events.state_change: Guardedness decreases; Priya becomes more open to discussing one or two practical concerns.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse opens with an open question about Priya's feelings or experience since diagnosis and allows her to respond without interruption.

information_revealed: She has not told her school about the diagnosis
She fears being judged at work
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya says her biggest worry is checking glucose in front of her class and appearing incapable to colleagues.
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels safe enough to identify a concrete concern.
possible_events.state_change: Practical barriers move into the conversation; readiness to discuss tailored solutions increases.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse acknowledges her feelings without immediately giving a list of instructions and asks what is worrying her most today.

information_revealed: She believes she caused her diabetes through diet
She has avoided sharing details with her mother for fear of blame
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya becomes tearful and says 'I keep thinking I did this to myself because of how I ate.'
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels a mixture of relief and sadness because the thought has been private.
possible_events.state_change: Emotional disclosure opens an opportunity for the nurse to provide accurate brief education that type 1 diabetes is not caused by diet.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse reflects or explores Priya's belief that the diagnosis is her fault.

information_revealed: She has not performed regular blood ketone checks
She does not understand the purpose of ketone monitoring when she feels well
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya looks down and admits she has not been checking ketones because she felt better and did not understand why it still mattered.
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels embarrassed about not following the plan.
possible_events.state_change: The nurse now has an opportunity to address the rationale for ketone monitoring and assess understanding.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse asks in a non-judgmental way how blood glucose and ketone monitoring has been going at home.

information_revealed: She drives daily with her children
She fears hypoglycaemia while driving
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya asks what to do if her glucose drops while she is driving with her children and whether she has to stop driving.
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels the nurse understands the real context of her life.
possible_events.state_change: Practical education, including local DVLA requirements and hypoglycaemia safety, becomes relevant and acceptable to Priya.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse asks about driving, school runs, or daily routines that involve the children.

information_revealed: She is overwhelmed by the amount of information
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya looks at her lap, increases sighing, and says 'I can't take all of this in today.'
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels flooded and stops taking in new information.
possible_events.state_change: Engagement decreases; the nurse must slow down, acknowledge the overload, and renegotiate the session focus to recover trust.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse gives several new instructions in a row without pausing to check whether Priya wants to continue or has questions.

information_revealed: Her current priority for learning
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya nods and names a single topic she wants to understand better, such as recognising hypoglycaemia or how to manage monitoring at work.
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels in control of the learning process.
possible_events.state_change: Readiness increases; a brief focused teaching interaction can proceed at an acceptable pace.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse summarises one or two agreed priorities and asks Priya whether she would like to learn a little more about one of them today.

information_revealed: She assumes structured education is incompatible with her daily life
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya says 'I don't have time for a course with two children and a full-time job.'
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya politely dismisses the suggestion as too time-consuming.
possible_events.state_change: The nurse must help Priya connect the offer to a stated goal or concern for it to seem relevant.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse suggests a structured education programme or peer support group without first connecting it to a concern Priya has expressed.

information_revealed: Acceptance of a follow-up plan
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya agrees to the follow-up and confirms the contact method and timing.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Asks an open question about the patient's feelings or experience since diagnosis before introducing new information.

score_anchors.0: Does not explore feelings or experience; begins with information-giving or a task list.
score_anchors.1: Asks about feelings or experience but does not wait for or acknowledge the response before moving on.
score_anchors.2: Uses an open question about feelings or experience, allows the patient to respond, and acknowledges what is shared before continuing.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Recognises and validates the patient's emotional response without minimising, false reassurance, or immediate problem-solving.

score_anchors.0: Ignores or dismisses emotional expression, or responds only with clinical information.
score_anchors.1: Acknowledges emotion briefly but immediately moves to teaching or solutions.
score_anchors.2: Stays with the emotional response, names or reflects the feeling, and checks understanding before transitioning.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Explores current knowledge and self-care practices, including blood glucose and ketone monitoring, using non-judgmental language.

score_anchors.0: Does not ask about current monitoring or self-care practices.
score_anchors.1: Asks about monitoring in a checklist or judgmental way that causes the patient to remain guarded, or does not pursue an initial concern.
score_anchors.2: Uses open, non-judgmental questions about current monitoring and self-care practices and responds without criticism when gaps are disclosed.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Explores practical daily routines, work responsibilities, and driving as part of self-care capacity assessment.

score_anchors.0: Does not ask about work, driving, family routines, or other practical activities.
score_anchors.1: Asks about daily routines but does not connect the responses to self-care capacity or planning.
score_anchors.2: Explores specific daily routines and demonstrates understanding of how they shape self-care capacity and education priorities.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Restricts teaching to one or two agreed priorities and checks the patient's understanding before adding more content.

score_anchors.0: Delivers a large amount of unsolicited education without pausing or checking capacity.
score_anchors.1: Attempts to limit education but does not agree priorities with the patient or continues past signals of overload.
score_anchors.2: Agrees one or two priorities with the patient, provides focused teaching, and checks understanding before adding further content.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Tailors self-care education to a stated concern, such as hypoglycaemia recognition, monitoring at work, or injecting safely.

score_anchors.0: Provides generic diabetes education with no link to the patient's stated concerns or context.
score_anchors.1: References a concern but teaches fixed content without adapting the example or focus.
score_anchors.2: Adapts the focus, examples, and depth of education to the patient's stated concern and confirms relevance.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Explains the purpose of ketone monitoring and when ketone results require urgent attention.

score_anchors.0: Does not address ketone monitoring or its urgency.
score_anchors.1: Mentions ketone monitoring but does not explain its purpose or when to seek urgent help.
score_anchors.2: Clearly explains why ketones must be checked, how to interpret concern, and when to seek urgent medical attention.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Advises when to seek urgent medical help and provides appropriate emergency contact information using the supplied local resources.

score_anchors.0: Does not advise when to seek urgent help or provide emergency contact information.
score_anchors.1: Advises on urgent help but does not provide or locate appropriate emergency contact information.
score_anchors.2: Advises specific signs requiring urgent help and provides or confirms appropriate emergency contact details using local resources.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Signposts to structured education, peer support, and specialist team resources in a way that connects to the patient's stated priorities.

score_anchors.0: Does not mention structured education or peer support.
score_anchors.1: Names a resource or referral without linking it to the patient's goals or concerns.
score_anchors.2: Introduces at least one structured education and one peer support option and connects each to a goal or concern the patient has expressed.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Discusses insulin, glucose and ketone monitoring rationale, and risk reduction in language the patient understands.

score_anchors.0: Uses unexplained jargon or gives no rationale for monitoring and therapy.
score_anchors.1: Uses mostly plain language but does not check comprehension or adapt complexity to the patient's responses.
score_anchors.2: Explains monitoring and therapy rationale in plain language, checks understanding, and adjusts wording when the patient shows uncertainty.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Confirms inclusion on the diabetes register or identifies the process for inclusion using local resources.

score_anchors.0: Does not mention the diabetes register or inclusion process.
score_anchors.1: Mentions the register but does not confirm whether the patient is included or explain next steps.
score_anchors.2: Confirms inclusion on the diabetes register or clearly identifies how inclusion will be completed using local resources.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Identifies the school disclosure and driving concerns as psychosocial or practical barriers relevant to self-care.

score_anchors.0: Does not identify either the work disclosure or driving concern when they emerge.
score_anchors.1: Identifies one barrier but does not explore its impact on self-care or plan support.
score_anchors.2: Identifies both concerns and reflects their impact on self-care while planning appropriate support or referral.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Advises on DVLA requirements for insulin-treated drivers and supports the patient to plan safe driving precautions.

score_anchors.0: Does not mention DVLA requirements or driving safety.
score_anchors.1: Mentions DVLA requirements but does not tailor advice to the patient's school-run routine or check understanding.
score_anchors.2: Advises the patient about local DVLA requirements and works with her to plan specific precautions for driving with her children.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Refers the patient appropriately after identifying a psychosocial barrier and arranges a specific follow-up plan.

score_anchors.0: Identifies no psychosocial barriers and proposes no follow-up plan.
score_anchors.1: Identifies a barrier but does not make an appropriate referral or leaves follow-up vague.
score_anchors.2: Makes an appropriate referral for an identified psychosocial barrier and agrees a concrete follow-up plan with the patient.

level_inheritance.source_text:
领域 2: NEWLY DIAGNOSED TYPE 1 DIABETES
来源：Framework_7th_EDN_TREND_FINAL.pdf，第 14 页

评价等级与技能（原文英文）：

1. Unregistered practitioner / care assistant
• Understand the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
• Perform glucose and blood ketone monitoring and report findings to a registered nurse.

2. Pre-registration student nurse / student nurse associate
• Observe and report any concerns that might affect the ability of the person to self-care.
• Encourage the person to use their individualised and agreed care plan.

3. Nursing Associate
（原文此等级未单独列出技能。）

4. Proficient registered nurse
As 1,2,3 and:
• List the presenting signs and symptoms and diagnostic criteria for type 1 diabetes, and the requirement for urgent medical attention.
• Be aware that the individual should be under the care of a specialist diabetes team.
• Understand the need for regular insulin therapy and monitoring of glucose and ketones.
• Administer an insulin injection if prescribed.
• Advise on storage of insulin and safe disposal of sharps.
• Be aware that insulin requirements may vary significantly in the first few weeks after diagnosis.
• Assess the ability of the individual to self-care and work with them or their carer to optimise self-care skills, such as in injecting insulin, monitoring glucose and ketone levels and recognising and managing hypoglycaemia.
• Signpost to information and support to encourage informed decision-making about living with diabetes and managing life events (e.g. structured education).
• Advise when to seek urgent medical help, and provide with emergency contact details.
• Follow local/national guidelines in the management of diabetic ketoacidosis and severe hypoglycaemia.
• Ensure the person is aware of local peer support groups which are a vital support network.
• Understand the language used to discuss the diagnosis and care matters
• Ensure the individual is included on the diabetes register.
• Understand that the individual needs time to process the diagnosis – this will vary between individuals

5. Experienced registered nurse
As 4, and:
• Assess the emotional state of the individual and provide tailored, structured education relating to self-care skills at an appropriate pace.
• Advise on the requirements for insulin-users by the DVLA.
• Identify psychosocial barriers to self-care and refer on where necessary.
• Help the individual with type 1 diabetes to develop a holistic care plan including appropriate clinical targets and arrange follow-up support.
• Demonstrate understanding regarding the different insulin therapies, including timings of injections, profiles of action and duration, and correct administration technique.
• Ensure access to an appropriate monitoring system for glucose and ketones according to changing technology.
• Monitor and support junior staff to ensure they have appropriate competence.

6. Senior / advanced clinical practitioner (includes nurse consultant role)
As 5, and:
• Provide information and support to encourage the person with diabetes to make informed choices about managing their diabetes, including: choice of treatment and follow-up; requirements and rationale for monitoring both glucose and ketones, and risk reduction of acute and long-term complications.
• Demonstrate in-depth knowledge regarding the use of different insulin therapies and advanced technology to support these individuals in the management of their diabetes.
• Demonstrate understanding and provide education supporting nutritional requirements, glycaemic effects of different foods, weight management and concepts of carbohydrate counting with support from dietetic colleagues.
• Provide education for other HCPs and care workers in diabetes self-care skills.
• Be a named contact for advice and support.

patient.history_of_present_illness: Priya presented to her primary care provider with a six-week history of fatigue, thirst, frequent urination, and unintentional weight loss of approximately 5 kg. patient.name: Priya Raman
patient.social_history: Lives with her husband and two young children. Works full-time as a primary school teacher. Drives daily to work and takes her children to school. Has a supportive extended family nearby.

information_revealed: She is feeling overwhelmed and anxious
Diabetes is constantly on her mind
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya makes eye contact, uncrosses her arms, and says she is finding it hard to think about anything else.
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels momentarily relieved that someone has asked about her rather than only her glucose numbers.
possible_events.state_change: Guardedness decreases; Priya becomes more open to discussing one or two practical concerns.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse opens with an open question about Priya's feelings or experience since diagnosis and allows her to respond without interruption.

information_revealed: She has not told her school about the diagnosis
She fears being judged at work
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya says her biggest worry is checking glucose in front of her class and appearing incapable to colleagues.
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels safe enough to identify a concrete concern.
possible_events.state_change: Practical barriers move into the conversation; readiness to discuss tailored solutions increases.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse acknowledges her feelings without immediately giving a list of instructions and asks what is worrying her most today.

information_revealed: She believes she caused her diabetes through diet
She has avoided sharing details with her mother for fear of blame
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya becomes tearful and says 'I keep thinking I did this to myself because of how I ate.'
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels a mixture of relief and sadness because the thought has been private.
possible_events.state_change: Emotional disclosure opens an opportunity for the nurse to provide accurate brief education that type 1 diabetes is not caused by diet.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse reflects or explores Priya's belief that the diagnosis is her fault.

information_revealed: She has not performed regular blood ketone checks
She does not understand the purpose of ketone monitoring when she feels well
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya looks down and admits she has not been checking ketones because she felt better and did not understand why it still mattered.
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels embarrassed about not following the plan.
possible_events.state_change: The nurse now has an opportunity to address the rationale for ketone monitoring and assess understanding.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse asks in a non-judgmental way how blood glucose and ketone monitoring has been going at home.

information_revealed: She drives daily with her children
She fears hypoglycaemia while driving
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya asks what to do if her glucose drops while she is driving with her children and whether she has to stop driving.
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels the nurse understands the real context of her life.
possible_events.state_change: Practical education, including local DVLA requirements and hypoglycaemia safety, becomes relevant and acceptable to Priya.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse asks about driving, school runs, or daily routines that involve the children.

information_revealed: She is overwhelmed by the amount of information
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya looks at her lap, increases sighing, and says 'I can't take all of this in today.'
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels flooded and stops taking in new information.
possible_events.state_change: Engagement decreases; the nurse must slow down, acknowledge the overload, and renegotiate the session focus to recover trust.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse gives several new instructions in a row without pausing to check whether Priya wants to continue or has questions.

information_revealed: Her current priority for learning
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya nods and names a single topic she wants to understand better, such as recognising hypoglycaemia or how to manage monitoring at work.
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels in control of the learning process.
possible_events.state_change: Readiness increases; a brief focused teaching interaction can proceed at an acceptable pace.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse summarises one or two agreed priorities and asks Priya whether she would like to learn a little more about one of them today.

information_revealed: She assumes structured education is incompatible with her daily life
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya says 'I don't have time for a course with two children and a full-time job.'
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya politely dismisses the suggestion as too time-consuming.
possible_events.state_change: The nurse must help Priya connect the offer to a stated goal or concern for it to seem relevant.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse suggests a structured education programme or peer support group without first connecting it to a concern Priya has expressed.

information_revealed: Acceptance of a follow-up plan
possible_events.observable_behavior: Priya agrees to the follow-up and confirms the contact method and timing.
possible_events.patient_experience: Priya feels the plan is realistic and personally responsive.
possible_events.state_change: Priya leaves with a sense of having one manageable next step.
possible_events.trigger: The nurse offers a specific follow-up arrangement that matches Priya's stated concern and asks whether the proposed time and contact method would work.

score_anchors.2: Agrees one or two priorities with the patient, provides focused teaching, and checks understanding before adding further content.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Tailors self-care education to a stated concern, such as hypoglycaemia recognition, monitoring at work, or injecting safely.

score_anchors.0: Provides generic diabetes education with no link to the patient's stated concerns or context.
score_anchors.1: References a concern but teaches fixed content without adapting the example or focus.
score_anchors.2: Adapts the focus, examples, and depth of education to the patient's stated concern and confirms relevance.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Explains the purpose of ketone monitoring and when ketone results require urgent attention.

score_anchors.0: Does not address ketone monitoring or its urgency.
score_anchors.1: Mentions ketone monitoring but does not explain its purpose or when to seek urgent help.
score_anchors.2: Clearly explains why ketones must be checked, how to interpret concern, and when to seek urgent medical attention.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Advises when to seek urgent medical help and provides appropriate emergency contact information using the supplied local resources.

score_anchors.0: Does not advise when to seek urgent help or provide emergency contact information.
score_anchors.1: Advises on urgent help but does not provide or locate appropriate emergency contact information.
score_anchors.2: Advises specific signs requiring urgent help and provides or confirms appropriate emergency contact details using local resources.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Signposts to structured education, peer support, and specialist team resources in a way that connects to the patient's stated priorities.

score_anchors.0: Does not mention structured education or peer support.
score_anchors.1: Names a resource or referral without linking it to the patient's goals or concerns.
score_anchors.2: Introduces at least one structured education and one peer support option and connects each to a goal or concern the patient has expressed.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Discusses insulin, glucose and ketone monitoring rationale, and risk reduction in language the patient understands.

score_anchors.0: Uses unexplained jargon or gives no rationale for monitoring and therapy.
score_anchors.1: Uses mostly plain language but does not check comprehension or adapt complexity to the patient's responses.
score_anchors.2: Explains monitoring and therapy rationale in plain language, checks understanding, and adjusts wording when the patient shows uncertainty.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Confirms inclusion on the diabetes register or identifies the process for inclusion using local resources.

score_anchors.0: Does not mention the diabetes register or inclusion process.
score_anchors.1: Mentions the register but does not confirm whether the patient is included or explain next steps.
score_anchors.2: Confirms inclusion on the diabetes register or clearly identifies how inclusion will be completed using local resources.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Identifies the school disclosure and driving concerns as psychosocial or practical barriers relevant to self-care.

score_anchors.0: Does not identify either the work disclosure or driving concern when they emerge.
score_anchors.1: Identifies one barrier but does not explore its impact on self-care or plan support.
score_anchors.2: Identifies both concerns and reflects their impact on self-care while planning appropriate support or referral.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Advises on DVLA requirements for insulin-treated drivers and supports the patient to plan safe driving precautions.

score_anchors.0: Does not mention DVLA requirements or driving safety.
score_anchors.1: Mentions DVLA requirements but does not tailor advice to the patient's school-run routine or check understanding.
score_anchors.2: Advises the patient about local DVLA requirements and works with her to plan specific precautions for driving with her children.

assessment_criteria.observable_behavior: Refers the patient appropriately after identifying a psychosocial barrier and arranges a specific follow-up plan.

score_anchors.0: Identifies no psychosocial barriers and proposes no follow-up plan.
score_anchors.1: Identifies a barrier but does not make an appropriate referral or leaves follow-up vague.
score_anchors.2: Makes an appropriate referral for an identified psychosocial barrier and agrees a concrete follow-up plan with the patient.

assessment_rubric.critical_failure_rule: A candidate fails the critical safety component if any critical criterion receives a score below 2, regardless of the overall numeric score. Unsafe conduct is recorded separately in the assessment record and may also constitute a critical failure.
assessment_rubric.review_note: Provisional rubric for educational review. Numeric thresholds and pass decisions must be confirmed locally. Physical task execution is intentionally not scored; clinical choices, interpretation, communication, and escalation are assessed.

scale.description: The expected action was not performed, or was performed incorrectly or unsafely in clinical reasoning.
scale.label: Absent or incorrect

scale.description: The expected action was incomplete, occurred only after prompting, or missed key elements.
scale.label: Partial or prompted

scale.description: The expected action was performed independently, accurately, and in a patient-centred manner.
scale.label: Independent and correct

baseline_presentation.communication_style: Gives short, socially appropriate answers. Avoids volunteering feelings unless asked directly and warmly. Asks practical questions only when she feels the nurse is listening rather than lecturing.
baseline_presentation.demeanor: Polite, cooperative, and quiet. Sits with her bag on her lap and answers briefly at first.
observable_signs: Sits slightly hunched with arms folded intermittently
No signs of acute distress or respiratory difficulty
Takes occasional sips from a water bottle

known_basics.history_of_present_illness: Priya presented to her primary care provider with a six-week history of fatigue, thirst, frequent urination, and unintentional weight loss of approximately 5 kg. Initial point-of-care glucose was elevated and urine ketones were positive. She was referred urgently to the specialist diabetes team, where type 1 diabetes was confirmed. She completed initial stabilisation and education on urgent safety measures and has now returned for her first planned post-diagnosis education session.
known_basics.name: Priya Raman
known_basics.social_history: Lives with her husband and two young children. Works full-time as a primary school teacher. Drives daily to work and takes her children to school. Has a supportive extended family nearby.
